# Summary: Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was an influential American computer scientist and electrical engineer known for pioneering work in microelectronics and VLSI design. After earning B.S. and M.S.E.E. degrees from Columbia University, Conway joined IBM Research in 1964 and contributed to the Advanced Computing Systems project, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling—an early superscalar design. Following her gender transition in 1968, which led to her dismissal from IBM, Conway restarted her career as a contract programmer and later held key roles at Memorex and Xerox PARC.
At Xerox PARC, she led the "LSI Systems" group and co-developed the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology with Carver Mead. This work revolutionized chip design, introduced dimensionless scalable design rules, and enabled rapid prototyping through the MOSIS system, profoundly influencing semiconductor design education and the industry. She also taught the pioneering MIT VLSI design course in 1978 and contributed to DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative. Conway held academic posts including professor and associate dean at the University of Michigan until her retirement in 1998.
Conway became a prominent transgender rights activist from the late 1990s onward, publicly sharing her transition story and advocating for trans inclusion, medical resources, and workplace protections. She coined the "Conway effect," describing how marginalized innovators are often overlooked historically. Her contributions earned numerous honors, including IEEE Fellow status, multiple prestigious awards (e.g., IEEE/RSE James Clerk Maxwell Medal), induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, and IBM’s Lifetime Achievement Award. Conway passed away on June 9, 2024, at age 86.
